meaning: Introduces your personal opinion, often one that is direct or slightly critical.
usage: Informal and spoken. Usually at the start of a sentence, but it can also come at the end: "It's far too expensive, if you ask me."
examples: If you ask me, the film was far too long.
If you ask me, they should have hired someone with more experience.
The new timetable makes no sense, if you ask me.
If you ask me, he's not as confident as he looks.

meaning: Signals that what follows is your own opinion, especially when others may see it differently.
usage: Neutral register. Often sounds firm or slightly defensive. Do not confuse it with "as far as … is concerned", which means "on the subject of".
examples: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
As far as I'm concerned, you can leave whenever you like.
As far as I'm concerned, honesty matters more than talent.
He can say what he wants; as far as I'm concerned, the decision was fair.

meaning: Introduces a frank opinion or admission, often one the listener may not want to hear.
usage: Very common in speech. Often softens criticism or a confession. Informal variant: "To be honest with you". Overusing it can make you sound as if you are not usually honest.
examples: To be honest, I didn't enjoy the party much.
To be honest, I haven't started the essay yet.
I'm not really sure, to be honest.
To be honest, I think we need a completely different approach.

meaning: Introduces your interpretation of a situation.
usage: Informal to neutral. Suggests that you have thought the matter through. Similar: "As I see it".
examples: The way I see it, we have two options.
The way I see it, the problem isn't money but time.
The way I see it, nobody is completely to blame.
The way I see it, you've got nothing to lose by applying.

meaning: Gives a cautious opinion or estimate.
usage: Common in speech and less forceful than "I think". Often used for estimates: "I'd say about fifty people came." Often followed by "that".
examples: I'd say the second option is slightly better.
I'd say there were about two hundred people there.
I'd say she's in her early forties.
If you want my advice, I'd say wait until the price drops.

meaning: Presents an opinion as a personal impression rather than a fact.
usage: Polite and slightly tentative, so it suits discussions and meetings. Can also end a sentence: "…, it seems to me."
examples: It seems to me that we're rushing this decision.
It seems to me that the real issue is communication.
It seems to me that he's not really interested in the job.
It seems to me that the plan has more risks than benefits.

meaning: Introduces an opinion based on your own position or experience.
usage: Neutral and common in discussions and essays. Often stresses your particular role: "From a teacher's point of view, …". Avoid the mixed form "in my point of view".
examples: From my point of view, the new system works much better.
From my point of view, the meeting was a complete waste of time.
From my point of view, the main benefit is flexibility.
From my point of view, it would be unfair to change the rules now.

meaning: Bases an opinion or generalization on what has happened to you personally.
usage: Makes a claim sound grounded rather than theoretical. Works in both speech and writing.
examples: In my experience, people work harder when they feel trusted.
In my experience, the cheapest option is rarely the best.
In my experience, language learners improve fastest when they travel.
In my experience, those meetings never finish on time.

meaning: Introduces your opinion.
usage: Slightly formal and more common in British English. Suits both speech and writing.
examples: To my mind, this is the best novel she has written.
To my mind, the decision was taken far too quickly.
To my mind, there's nothing wrong with changing your plans.
To my mind, the city has lost a lot of its character.

meaning: Expresses a general or mild opinion rather than a strong conviction.
usage: Softer than "I think" and useful for disagreeing politely. Often followed by "that".
examples: I tend to think that people are basically good.
I tend to think small schools are better for younger children.
I tend to think the problem is exaggerated.
Personally, I tend to think he made the right choice.

meaning: States an opinion you hold with complete certainty.
usage: Strong and confident. Weaker alternatives: "I'm fairly sure that", "I suspect that".
examples: I'm convinced that he's telling the truth.
I'm convinced that this approach will save us money.
Whatever the experts say, I'm convinced that the test results were wrong.
I'm convinced that we'll look back on this as a turning point.

meaning: Expresses a firm opinion, often one about values or principles.
usage: Common in debates, speeches and opinion essays. "Firmly believe" is a close alternative.
examples: I strongly believe that education should be free.
I strongly believe that everyone deserves a second chance.
I strongly believe that the policy will harm small businesses.
I strongly believe that children learn best through play.

meaning: Expresses an intuition or suspicion that you cannot fully justify.
usage: Often followed by "that". Common variants: "I've got a feeling" and "I have a funny feeling", for a slightly worrying suspicion.
examples: I have a feeling we've met before.
I have a feeling that it's going to rain later.
I have a feeling she won't accept the offer.
I have a feeling something's wrong; she hasn't replied all day.

meaning: Introduces an instinctive judgement rather than a reasoned one.
usage: Informal. Often used when there is not enough information to be sure. Related: "go with your gut", meaning to trust your instinct.
examples: My gut feeling is that we should wait.
My gut feeling is that he's hiding something.
I can't prove it, but my gut feeling is that the deal will fall through.
My gut feeling is that the second candidate is a better fit.

meaning: Expresses a thought or doubt that you cannot ignore, even if you would like to.
usage: Often introduces a mild criticism or worry. Followed by "(that)" and a clause. Similar: "I can't help feeling".
examples: I can't help thinking we've made a mistake.
I can't help thinking that she deserved the promotion more.
I can't help thinking there's more to this story.
I can't help thinking that the price is a little too good to be true.

meaning: Shows strong support for an idea, often before adding a reservation.
usage: Informal. Followed by a noun or -ing form. Often followed by "but": "I'm all for saving money, but …".
examples: I'm all for working from home, but I miss my colleagues.
I'm all for new ideas, as long as they're practical.
If it helps the environment, I'm all for it.
I'm all for giving young people more responsibility.

chunk: I'm not a big fan of …
meaning: A mild, polite way to say that you do not like something.
usage: Informal. Softer than "I don't like". Followed by a noun or -ing form.
examples: I'm not a big fan of horror films.
I'm not a big fan of working late.
To be honest, I'm not a big fan of open-plan offices.
I'm not a big fan of spicy food, so I'll have the soup.

meaning: Expresses a preference for one action over another.
usage: Followed by a bare infinitive: "I'd rather walk than drive." The "than" part can be omitted when it is clear. Note the past form with another subject: "I'd rather you didn't."
examples: I'd rather stay in tonight than go to a noisy bar.
I'd rather pay a bit more than wait three weeks.
I'd rather work alone than in a big group.
Honestly, I'd rather do it myself than explain it to someone else.

meaning: Says that an action would be useless or achieve nothing.
usage: Followed by an -ing form. Also: "There's no point (in) arguing about it." Related: "What's the point of …?".
examples: There's no point in arguing about it now.
There's no point in buying a car if you never drive.
There's no point in worrying about things you can't change.
There's no point in waiting; the bus has already gone.

chunk: I don't see the point of …
meaning: Expresses doubt that something is useful or worth doing.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Can sound critical or dismissive.
examples: I don't see the point of having a meeting if nobody prepares.
I don't see the point of buying expensive trainers.
I don't see the point of the new rules.
I don't see the point of learning grammar rules by heart.

meaning: Focuses attention on the feature you appreciate most in something.
usage: A cleft sentence that puts emphasis on the final part. Also: "What I don't like about … is …".
examples: What I like about this city is that everything is within walking distance.
What I like about her teaching is that she's so patient.
What I like about the job is the variety.
What I like about living alone is the freedom.

meaning: Introduces the main weakness or drawback of something.
usage: Very common in discussion. Usually followed by "that" and a clause, or by a noun.
examples: The problem with this plan is that it's too expensive.
The problem with social media is that it's so addictive.
The problem with cheap shoes is they don't last.
The problem with him is that he never listens.

meaning: Asks for someone's opinion or interpretation.
usage: Informal and conversational. A "take" is a particular view of something.
examples: What's your take on the new manager?
What's your take on the election results?
Before we decide, what's your take on the budget?
So, what's your take on remote working?

meaning: Asks someone how they understand or judge something, often something puzzling.
usage: Informal. Often used about surprising behaviour or news. Answer pattern: "I don't know what to make of it."
examples: What do you make of his sudden resignation?
What do you make of the new design?
What do you make of these results?
She left without saying goodbye. What do you make of that?

meaning: Asks for someone's opinion or emotional reaction to something.
usage: Polite and open. Often used before a proposal: "How do you feel about starting earlier?" Followed by a noun or -ing form.
examples: How do you feel about moving to another city?
How do you feel about the changes to the course?
How do you feel about working at weekends?
How do you feel about the idea of a four-day week?

meaning: Asks for someone's position on an issue, often a controversial one.
usage: Common with political, ethical or social topics. Answer: "I'm firmly against it" or "I'm in favour".
examples: Where do you stand on nuclear power?
Where do you stand on the issue of school uniforms?
Before we vote, where do you stand on this?
Where do you stand on raising the minimum wage?

meaning: States an opinion in a formal way.
usage: Formal and slightly old-fashioned in conversation. It suits debates, letters and formal discussions.
examples: I'm of the opinion that the project should be postponed.
I'm of the opinion that exams are not the best way to assess students.
Having read the report, I'm of the opinion that further funding is justified.
I'm of the opinion that we should consult the staff first.

meaning: Says that something is useful, valuable or deserves the effort.
usage: Followed by an -ing form ("It's worth visiting") or a noun ("It's worth a try"). Also: "It's worth it" and, for emphasis, "well worth".
examples: It's worth checking the reviews before you book.
The museum is small, but it's worth a visit.
It's worth asking whether there's a student discount.
It was expensive, but it's worth every penny.

meaning: Marks an opinion clearly as your own, often in contrast to what others think.
usage: Common in discussions. "Personally" is usually followed by a comma in writing.
examples: Personally, I think the book is better than the film.
Personally, I think we should wait another year.
Personally, I think it's a great idea, but not everyone agrees.
Personally, I think honesty is the most important quality in a friend.

meaning: Expresses a long-held belief or view.
usage: Often introduces an opinion that has just been confirmed or challenged. Often followed by "that".
examples: I've always thought that she'd make a great teacher.
I've always thought it was a strange rule.
I've always thought London was too expensive, and I still do.
I've always thought people underestimate how hard that job is.

meaning: Expresses complete agreement.
usage: Despite the negative form, it means “I agree completely”. Neutral register and suitable for meetings. Can be followed by “with you” or “with what you said”.
examples: “We need more time to prepare.” “I couldn't agree more.”
I couldn't agree more with what Sarah just said.
“Exercise is the best medicine.” “I couldn't agree more.”
I couldn't agree more; the system needs a complete overhaul.

meaning: Expresses strong agreement, usually with a complaint or obvious truth.
usage: Informal and spoken. Usually a reply to a comment about something unpleasant, such as weather, prices or tiredness.
examples: “It's freezing today.” “You can say that again!”
“That exam was brutal.” “You can say that again.”
“Rents in this city are ridiculous.” “You can say that again.”
“He talks a lot, doesn't he?” “You can say that again.”

meaning: Shows that you know exactly what someone means because you have experienced it too.
usage: Informal and spoken, said with falling intonation. It does not ask for more information; it signals shared frustration.
examples: “The traffic was awful this morning.” “Tell me about it. I was stuck for an hour.”
“Teenagers can be so moody.” “Tell me about it. I've got three.”
“This printer never works.” “Tell me about it.”
“I'm exhausted.” “Tell me about it. I've been up since five.”

meaning: Says that you share someone's opinion on a particular point.
usage: Informal to neutral. Often used to agree with one point while staying neutral about others.
examples: “We should ask for feedback earlier.” “I'm with you on that.”
I'm with you on that; the deadline is unrealistic.
“The rules are too complicated.” “I'm with you on that one.”
I'm with you on that, but I'm not sure the others will agree.

chunk: That's exactly what I was thinking
meaning: Says that someone has expressed the same idea you had.
usage: Informal and enthusiastic. Variant: “That's just what I was thinking.”
examples: “Shall we just order pizza?” “That's exactly what I was thinking.”
“Maybe the problem is the software, not the computer.” “That's exactly what I was thinking.”
That's exactly what I was thinking when I read the report.
“We should leave early to avoid the traffic.” “That's exactly what I was thinking.”

meaning: Admits that what someone has said is reasonable, often after you initially disagreed.
usage: Informal. Often followed by “there”. More formal: “You have a point.”
examples: “It would be cheaper to take the train.” “You've got a point there.”
You've got a point; we haven't really considered the cost.
“Maybe she didn't get your message.” “Hmm, you've got a point.”
I suppose you've got a point, but I still don't like the idea.

meaning: Accepts that someone's argument or objection is reasonable.
usage: Informal and concise. Often used to concede a point in a discussion. Also: “That's a fair point.”
examples: “We can't afford to hire anyone else.” “Fair point.”
Fair point, but we still need someone to manage the project.
“You haven't asked her what she thinks.” “That's a fair point.”
Fair point; I hadn't thought about the time difference.

meaning: Agrees with a suggestion or view, often without great enthusiasm.
usage: Neutral. Often signals acceptance rather than strong support: you are willing to accept it.
examples: “Let's meet on Thursday instead.” “I'd go along with that.”
If everyone else is happy, I'd go along with that.
I'd go along with that, as long as the budget stays the same.
“The second design is clearer.” “Yes, I'd go along with that.”

meaning: Agrees reluctantly, often after some resistance.
usage: Signals that you accept the argument but are not happy about it. Variant: “I guess you're right.”
examples: “You need to rest, not go to the gym.” “I suppose you're right.”
I suppose you're right; it's too late to change the plan now.
“It's not worth fixing that old laptop.” “I suppose you're right.”
I suppose you're right, but I'll miss the old office.

meaning: Accepts part of an argument while suggesting it is not the whole picture.
usage: Diplomatic partial agreement. Often followed by “but”. Stronger: “There's a lot of truth in that.”
examples: “Social media makes people lonelier.” “There's some truth in that.”
There's some truth in that, but it's not the only reason.
“Exams only test memory.” “Well, there's some truth in that.”
I think there's some truth in that, although the data is mixed.

chunk: I see what you mean, but …
meaning: Shows that you understand someone's view before politely disagreeing.
usage: A standard way to soften disagreement in conversation and meetings.
examples: I see what you mean, but I think the risks are too high.
I see what you mean, but that's not quite what happened.
I see what you mean, but we've tried that before.
I see what you mean, but not everyone can afford to travel.

meaning: Accepts that someone has made a valid argument before introducing an objection.
usage: Neutral to formal and common in meetings and debates. Also: “Point taken.”
examples: I take your point, but we can't delay the launch again.
I take your point, but the figures tell a different story.
I take your point, but I still think we should ask the client first.
I take your point, but safety has to come first.

meaning: Concedes that a statement could be correct while arguing that it is not decisive.
usage: Common in discussions and essays. Variant: “That might be true, but …”.
examples: That may be true, but it doesn't solve the problem.
That may be true, but most people can't afford it.
That may be true, but it's not what the client asked for.
“Cars are more convenient.” “That may be true, but they're also much more expensive.”

meaning: Says that something is partly true and partly false.
usage: Usually followed by an explanation of both sides. Useful when a simple answer would be misleading.
examples: “Did you enjoy the course?” “Yes and no. The content was good, but the teacher wasn't.”
“Is it cheaper to live outside the city?” “Yes and no.”
Yes and no; it depends on what you mean by success.
“So, was the trip a success?” “Yes and no.”

meaning: Shows partial agreement: something is true to a limited extent.
usage: Often used as a short reply, or in “I agree with you up to a point”. Similar: “to some extent”.
examples: “Money can't buy happiness.” “Up to a point.”
I agree with you up to a point, but there are exceptions.
The strategy worked up to a point, then sales levelled off.
Up to a point, practice makes perfect; after that, you need feedback.

meaning: Says that someone's statement is too strong or exaggerated, although partly true.
usage: Polite partial disagreement. Often followed by a milder version of the claim.
examples: “The film was a disaster.” “I wouldn't go that far. It had some good moments.”
“He's a genius.” “Well, I wouldn't go that far.”
I wouldn't go that far, but it certainly wasn't his best work.
“The project has completely failed.” “I wouldn't go that far.”

meaning: Says that something is not always or automatically true.
usage: A short, polite way to challenge a generalization. Often followed by an example or explanation.
examples: “Expensive wine tastes better.” “Not necessarily.”
“A degree guarantees you a good job.” “Not necessarily.”
“If it's popular, it must be good.” “Not necessarily.”
Not necessarily; some of the best restaurants are the cheapest.

meaning: Challenges a generalization by pointing out that there are exceptions.
usage: Polite and neutral. Common in discussions and academic speech.
examples: “Older people find technology difficult.” “That's not always the case.”
That's not always the case; some small firms pay very well.
People assume bigger is better, but that's not always the case.
That's not always the case, as my own experience shows.

chunk: I'm not so sure about that
meaning: Expresses doubt about what someone has said; a gentle way to disagree.
usage: Polite and informal. Softer than “I disagree”.
examples: “The weather will be fine tomorrow.” “I'm not so sure about that.”
I'm not so sure about that; the forecast says rain.
“Everyone will love the new logo.” “Hmm, I'm not so sure about that.”
I'm not so sure about that. Have you checked the figures?

meaning: Expresses doubt about a claim or plan.
usage: Neutral to formal and common in meetings and academic discussion. Also: “I'm not convinced” on its own.
examples: I'm not convinced that this is the right time to invest.
I'm not convinced that the new policy will make any difference.
I'm not convinced that he understood the question.
I'm not convinced that working longer hours makes us more productive.

meaning: Says that you cannot decide what you think or what to do.
usage: Mainly British. Followed by a noun, an -ing form or “whether”. American English prefers “I'm torn about …”.
examples: I'm in two minds about whether to accept the job.
I'm in two minds about the new design.
I'm in two minds about going to the party.
I'm in two minds about it; both options have their advantages.

meaning: Politely says that you have a different opinion.
usage: Neutral and diplomatic. Often followed by an explanation.
examples: I respect your view, but I see things differently.
I see things differently; I think the problem is the management.
My parents think I should study law, but I see things differently.
“Everyone says the plan is brilliant.” “I see things differently. It's far too risky.”

chunk: That's not how I see it
meaning: States clearly that you disagree with someone's interpretation.
usage: Fairly direct but still polite. Often followed by your own interpretation.
examples: “You lost because you didn't train.” “That's not how I see it.”
That's not how I see it; the decision was made before I joined.
I understand why you're angry, but that's not how I see it.
That's not how I see it at all.

meaning: A polite but clear way to express disagreement.
usage: “I'm afraid” softens the message. Common in formal discussions and meetings.
examples: I'm afraid I disagree; the data doesn't support that.
I'm afraid I disagree with you on this point.
I'm afraid I disagree. I think we should wait.
With respect, I'm afraid I disagree.

meaning: Expresses total disagreement.
usage: Very strong. The opposite of “I couldn't agree more”. Use with care in formal settings.
examples: “Teachers have an easy job.” “I couldn't disagree more.”
I couldn't disagree more with that decision.
I couldn't disagree more; this is the worst possible time to cut costs.
“Art is a waste of time.” “I couldn't disagree more.”

meaning: A formal phrase used before disagreeing with or criticizing someone.
usage: Formal. Despite its polite form, it often signals strong disagreement and can sound cold or annoyed.
examples: With all due respect, I don't think you've read the report.
With all due respect, that's not your decision to make.
With all due respect, the figures say otherwise.
With all due respect, sir, we've already tried that.

meaning: Says that something is not relevant to the issue being discussed.
usage: Can sound impatient. Often used to steer a discussion back to the main issue.
examples: “But it was cheap!” “That's beside the point. It doesn't work.”
“He didn't mean to upset her.” “That's beside the point; he still did.”
That's beside the point; we're talking about the budget.
“But she's my friend.” “That's beside the point. Rules are rules.”

chunk: That's one way of looking at it
meaning: Implies that you see the matter differently, without saying so directly.
usage: Diplomatic and sometimes slightly ironic. Often a polite signal of disagreement.
examples: “I didn't fail; I just didn't pass.” “Well, that's one way of looking at it.”
That's one way of looking at it, but there are others.
“Losing my job gave me more free time.” “That's one way of looking at it.”
I suppose that's one way of looking at it.

meaning: Ends an argument by accepting that neither side will change their mind.
usage: Friendly and conciliatory. Also: “We'll have to agree to disagree.”
examples: We're never going to settle this, so let's agree to disagree.
Let's agree to disagree and talk about something else.
OK, let's agree to disagree on that one.
We've both made our points; let's agree to disagree.

meaning: Expresses shock or disbelief at what someone has said.
usage: Informal and emotional. Can show disagreement or simply surprise. Also: “You're not serious!”
examples: “I'm quitting my job tomorrow.” “You can't be serious!”
You can't be serious! That's twice the price.
“They want us to finish by Friday.” “You can't be serious.”
You can't be serious about moving to Antarctica.

meaning: Presents information as an impression or conclusion rather than a certain fact.
usage: Neutral and common in both speech and writing. More tentative than a plain statement. Also: “It would seem that …” (more formal).
examples: It seems that nobody told her about the meeting.
It seems that the problem started after the update.
It seems that more people are cycling to work these days.
From the evidence, it seems that the fire started in the kitchen.

meaning: Describes what appears to be happening or likely to happen, based on what you can see.
usage: Neutral. Informal alternative: “It looks like …”. Usually followed by a full clause.
examples: It looks as if it's going to rain.
It looks as if they've already left.
It looks as if the price will go up again next year.
It looks as if we'll have to start again from scratch.

meaning: Softens a statement or opinion by admitting you could be mistaken.
usage: Polite and modest. It often introduces something you are fairly sure about.
examples: I might be wrong, but I think the shop closes at six.
I might be wrong, but wasn't the meeting moved to Friday?
I might be wrong, but she didn't seem very happy.
I might be wrong, but I don't think this is the right road.

chunk: Correct me if I'm wrong, but …
meaning: Introduces a statement politely while inviting the listener to correct it.
usage: Common in meetings. It can also be a polite way to challenge someone: “Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't you agree to this?”
examples: Correct me if I'm wrong, but the deadline is next Monday, isn't it?
Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't you say you'd call them?
Correct me if I'm wrong, but this is the third time this month.
Correct me if I'm wrong, but I think we've met before.

meaning: Signals that you are fairly but not completely certain.
usage: Polite and precise. “Entirely” softens the uncertainty; you are mostly sure.
examples: I'm not entirely sure, but I think it starts at eight.
I'm not entirely sure, but I believe she's on holiday.
I'm not entirely sure, but the answer might be in chapter three.
I'm not entirely sure, but I don't think parking is free here.

meaning: Introduces a fact you believe is correct while allowing for error.
usage: Polite and slightly formal. Can come at the start or end of a sentence.
examples: If I'm not mistaken, this building used to be a cinema.
If I'm not mistaken, you studied in Edinburgh.
The train leaves at 9.15, if I'm not mistaken.
If I'm not mistaken, we've already paid that invoice.

meaning: Introduces something you think you remember, while admitting your memory may be wrong.
usage: Mainly British. Variants: “If I remember correctly” and “If memory serves”.
examples: If I remember rightly, the restaurant is next to the bank.
If I remember rightly, she has two brothers.
We met in 2015, if I remember rightly.
If I remember rightly, the exam was much easier last year.

meaning: Says that something is true according to your knowledge, which may be incomplete.
usage: Neutral and very common. Can come at the start or end of a sentence.
examples: As far as I know, the library is open on Sundays.
As far as I know, nobody has complained.
He's still working there, as far as I know.
As far as I know, the offer is still available.

chunk: As far as I can tell, …
meaning: Gives a judgement based on what you can observe or understand.
usage: Neutral. Suggests that you are judging from limited evidence. Similar: “As far as I can see”.
examples: As far as I can tell, there's nothing wrong with the engine.
As far as I can tell, they're getting on well.
The instructions are correct, as far as I can tell.
As far as I can tell, the problem only affects older phones.

meaning: Says that you believe something, often when you suspect you may have misunderstood.
usage: Neutral to formal. Past form is common when you discover you were wrong: “I was under the impression that …”.
examples: I'm under the impression that the meeting has been cancelled.
I'm under the impression that she wants to leave the company.
I'm under the impression that the price includes breakfast. Is that right?
I'm under the impression that we agreed on a smaller budget.

meaning: Expresses a belief that something is probably true, usually something negative or hidden.
usage: Neutral. The word “that” is often dropped in speech. Stronger than “I think” in suggesting hidden truth.
examples: I suspect that he already knows the answer.
I suspect that the real reason is money.
I suspect that most people never read the terms and conditions.
I suspect that the delay will be longer than they say.

meaning: Offers a prediction or estimate that is not based on firm evidence.
usage: Informal to neutral. Often used when someone asks a question you cannot answer with certainty.
examples: My guess is that they'll announce the results next week.
My guess is that she forgot.
My guess is that prices will keep rising for a while.
My guess is that he took the earlier train.

meaning: Says that something is likely.
usage: Informal. Followed by a clause, sometimes with “that”. Also: “The chances are …”.
examples: Chances are she's already at home.
If you leave now, chances are you'll miss the traffic.
Chances are that the shop will be closed by the time we get there.
Chances are you've heard this story before.

meaning: Says that something is quite likely.
usage: Usually followed by “(that)” and a clause, or by “of”. Stronger: “There's every chance …”; weaker: “There's a slight chance …”.
examples: There's a good chance it'll be sunny tomorrow.
There's a good chance that the flight will be delayed.
There's a good chance of finding a cheaper hotel online.
If we apply early, there's a good chance we'll get a place.

meaning: Predicts that something is quite likely, often something unexpected or unwelcome.
usage: Informal to neutral. Often followed by a past tense or “would”, but present tenses are also common.
examples: I wouldn't be surprised if they got married next year.
I wouldn't be surprised if the concert sold out.
I wouldn't be surprised if he didn't turn up.
I wouldn't be surprised if prices doubled by the summer.

meaning: Says that you think something is unlikely or untrue.
usage: Neutral. “That” is often dropped. Alternatives: “I doubt whether …”, “I doubt it.”
examples: I doubt that they'll finish on time.
I doubt that anyone noticed the mistake.
I doubt that he'll change his mind.
I doubt that the shop is still open.

meaning: Says that you cannot give a clear answer or prediction.
usage: Common reply to a difficult question. Can be followed by a question word: “It's hard to say why.”
examples: “Will the project succeed?” “It's hard to say.”
It's hard to say how long the repairs will take.
It's hard to say who's right in this situation.
It's hard to say at this stage; we need more data.

meaning: Says that the answer to a question varies according to a particular factor.
usage: Very common. Followed by a noun or a question word clause: “It depends on how much it costs.” Also on its own: “It depends.”
examples: It depends on the weather.
It depends on how much time we have.
“Will you come?” “It depends on whether I finish work early.”
“Is it worth buying a car?” “It depends on where you live.”

meaning: Partly, but not completely.
usage: Common in essays and discussions. Similar: “to a certain extent”. Stronger: “to a large extent”.
examples: I agree with you to some extent.
To some extent, the crisis was caused by poor planning.
Success depends to some extent on luck.
The new rules have worked to some extent, but problems remain.

meaning: Partly, or when you consider it from a certain angle.
usage: Informal. Often softens a surprising or unusual idea. Also: “in some ways”.
examples: In a way, losing that job was the best thing that happened to me.
He's right, in a way.
In a way, I'm glad it rained; we got to stay in and talk.
The ending was sad, but in a way it was also hopeful.

meaning: Almost, approximately or nearly completely.
usage: Informal. Can modify adjectives, verbs and numbers: “more or less finished”, “more or less fifty”.
examples: The work is more or less finished.
We more or less agree on the main points.
It took more or less an hour to get there.
That's more or less what I expected.

meaning: Somewhat or slightly; used to make a statement less direct.
usage: Informal and spoken. Avoid it in formal writing. Also: “sort of” (more British).
examples: I'm kind of tired, so I'll go home early.
It was kind of strange to see him again.
I kind of agree with you, but not completely.
The film was kind of boring in the middle.

meaning: Introduces a statement you think is reasonable and not exaggerated.
usage: Common in discussions and journalism. Often used for a cautious judgement or an understatement.
examples: It's fair to say that the launch didn't go as planned.
It's fair to say that she's had a difficult year.
It's fair to say that technology has changed the way we learn.
It's fair to say that not everyone was happy with the result.

meaning: Introduces a general statement that is true in most cases but not in every detail.
usage: Neutral to formal. Suits essays and presentations. Similar: “In general”.
examples: Broadly speaking, there are two types of learners.
Broadly speaking, the results were positive.
Broadly speaking, prices are lower outside the city centre.
Broadly speaking, I agree with your proposal.

meaning: Introduces a statement that is usually true, while allowing for exceptions.
usage: Neutral. Common in both speech and writing.
examples: Generally speaking, the trains here are very reliable.
Generally speaking, women live longer than men.
Generally speaking, it's cheaper to book in advance.
Generally speaking, our customers are very satisfied.

meaning: Mostly or in most respects.
usage: Neutral. Common in reviews and evaluations, often followed by a qualification.
examples: For the most part, the students were well prepared.
The holiday was, for the most part, very relaxing.
For the most part, I enjoy my job.
For the most part, the changes have been welcomed.

meaning: Says that something is usually true, but not always.
usage: Neutral and common in instructions, reports and explanations.
examples: In most cases, the problem can be fixed by restarting the computer.
In most cases, patients recover within a week.
In most cases, the cheapest flights leave very early.
In most cases, a short email is more effective than a long one.

meaning: Introduces a general conclusion after considering everything.
usage: Neutral, especially British. Often used for an overall judgement despite some problems.
examples: On the whole, the trip was a success.
On the whole, I prefer living in the countryside.
There were a few problems, but on the whole it went well.
On the whole, the reviews have been positive.

meaning: Describes what usually happens or what you normally do.
usage: Neutral. Often describes personal habits: “As a rule, I don't drink coffee after lunch.”
examples: As a rule, I don't check emails at the weekend.
As a rule, the first lesson is free.
As a rule, the trains are on time, but not today.
As a rule, we don't give refunds on sale items.

meaning: Suggests a possible explanation without claiming it is certain.
usage: Neutral. Useful when speculating about causes. Also: “It may be that …” (more formal).
examples: It could be that she didn't receive the email.
It could be that the battery is dead.
It could be that people are simply too busy to reply.
It could be that the instructions were unclear.

meaning: Adds another point, usually one that makes a situation better or, more often, worse.
usage: Informal to neutral, and common in speech. More formal alternatives: “In addition”, “Moreover”.
examples: The hotel was dirty. On top of that, the staff were rude.
I lost my wallet, and on top of that I missed the last bus.
The job pays well. On top of that, you get six weeks' holiday.
We're short of staff, and on top of that two people are off sick.

meaning: Adds a further, often stronger, point to support what you have just said.
usage: Neutral. Common in speech and less formal writing. Formal equivalent: “Furthermore”.
examples: The flat is cheap. What's more, it's close to the station.
She speaks four languages. What's more, she's only nineteen.
The plan is risky, and what's more, it's expensive.
This laptop is light, and what's more, the battery lasts all day.

meaning: Adds a further point that strengthens your argument, often one that is obvious.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Usually comes after a comma at the end of a list.
examples: Driving into town takes ages, not to mention the cost of parking.
She's clever and funny, not to mention very kind.
The house needs a new roof, not to mention new windows.
Moving abroad is stressful, not to mention expensive.

meaning: Emphasizes that two things are true, especially when the second is surprising.
usage: Both parts should have the same grammatical form. At the start of a sentence it requires inversion: “Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.”
examples: The course is not only useful but also enjoyable.
He not only finished the report but also prepared the slides.
The new system is not only faster but also more reliable.
Cycling is not only cheap but also good for your health.

meaning: Means either “except for” or “in addition to”, depending on the context.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. “Apart from that” is a common way to add a contrast: “It rained a bit. Apart from that, it was perfect.”
examples: Apart from the weather, the holiday was perfect.
Apart from English, she speaks French and Arabic.
Apart from working full-time, he's also studying for a degree.
The room was a bit small. Apart from that, everything was fine.

meaning: Adds something to what you have already mentioned; means “and also”.
usage: Followed by a noun or an -ing form, not a full clause: “as well as working”, not “as well as she works”.
examples: She teaches maths as well as science.
As well as working full-time, he volunteers at weekends.
The price includes breakfast as well as dinner.
We need to consider the cost as well as the benefits.

meaning: Introduces a point that contrasts with or limits what you have just said.
usage: Neutral to formal. Very close to “Having said that”.
examples: The hotel is expensive. That being said, the service is excellent.
I love my job. That being said, I wouldn't mind earning more.
The results are encouraging. That being said, more research is needed.
He can be difficult. That being said, he's very good at what he does.

meaning: Introduces a contrasting point after something you have just said.
usage: Common in British speech. Often follows a positive or negative statement with a qualification.
examples: The film is too long. Having said that, I really enjoyed it.
I don't usually like spicy food. Having said that, this curry is delicious.
The exam was hard. Having said that, I think I did quite well.
It's a great city. Having said that, I wouldn't want to live there.

meaning: Introduces something that is true despite what has just been said.
usage: Neutral. Similar to “nevertheless” but less formal.
examples: The flat was small. Even so, it felt very comfortable.
He apologized. Even so, she was still angry.
The odds were against us. Even so, we decided to try.
It's an old car. Even so, it's never let me down.

meaning: Means “despite this”; introduces something that remains true.
usage: Informal to neutral, often British. Also at the end of a sentence: “Thanks all the same.”
examples: I know it's safe. All the same, I'd rather not go alone.
It wasn't a perfect performance. All the same, the audience loved it.
He's probably right. All the same, I'd like a second opinion.
I didn't need any help, but thanks all the same.

meaning: Introduces a contrasting point or the opposite side of an argument.
usage: Often paired with “On the one hand”. Do not use it simply to add information; it must show contrast.
examples: City life is exciting. On the other hand, it can be very stressful.
The job is well paid. On the other hand, the hours are long.
On the one hand, I'd like to travel; on the other hand, I need to save money.
Online courses are flexible. On the other hand, they can feel isolating.

meaning: Introduces a thought that makes you reconsider or weaken what you have just said.
usage: Informal and spoken. Often used when thinking aloud. Similar: “But then again”.
examples: The restaurant is expensive. Then again, the food is amazing.
I might take the job. Then again, I might not.
He's very young for the role. Then again, so was I at his age.
It looks difficult. But then again, everything is at first.

meaning: Introduces a fact that contrasts with the main clause.
usage: Neutral to formal. “Despite” cannot be followed directly by a clause, so “the fact that” is needed. Shorter alternative: “although”.
examples: She went to work despite the fact that she was ill.
Despite the fact that it was raining, the match went ahead.
He got the job despite the fact that he had no experience.
Despite the fact that prices have risen, sales remain strong.

meaning: Introduces a contrast that makes the main statement surprising.
usage: Stronger than “although”. Do not confuse it with “even if”, which introduces a hypothetical situation.
examples: Even though it was late, the shop was still busy.
He kept running even though his leg hurt.
I enjoyed the film even though I didn't understand the ending.
Even though she studied hard, she didn't pass.

meaning: Introduces the consequence of something.
usage: Neutral. Common in both speech and writing. Related: “as a result of” + noun.
examples: The trains were cancelled. As a result, many people were late for work.
He trained every day and, as a result, he won the race.
Prices rose sharply. As a result, demand fell.
She missed several classes and, as a result, failed the exam.

meaning: Introduces the result or explanation of something just mentioned.
usage: Informal to neutral and very common in speech. In formal writing, prefer “This is why” or “For this reason”.
examples: I didn't sleep well. That's why I'm so tired.
The bus was late; that's why I missed the start.
She's very patient. That's why the children love her.
We want to reduce waste, and that's why we've stopped using plastic bags.

meaning: Introduces the reason for something; means “because”.
usage: Formal and wordy. In most writing, “because” or “as” is clearer. Common in official notices.
examples: The event was cancelled due to the fact that too few people had registered.
Due to the fact that the road is closed, buses will take a different route.
Delays occurred due to the fact that the supplier went out of business.
Prices have increased due to the fact that energy costs have risen.

meaning: Introduces the purpose of an action.
usage: Often followed by a modal verb: “so that we could”, “so that she can”. In informal speech, “that” is often dropped.
examples: I left early so that I could avoid the traffic.
Speak clearly so that everyone can hear you.
We moved the meeting so that more people could attend.
She saved money every month so that she could travel.

meaning: Expresses purpose; means “to” or “so that”.
usage: More formal than “to” alone. Negative: “in order not to”.
examples: She took a part-time job in order to pay her fees.
In order to apply, you need to fill in this form.
In order to save time, we took a taxi.
The company cut costs in order to stay competitive.

meaning: Means “only if” or “on condition that”.
usage: Followed by a present tense for future meaning: “as long as you finish”, not “as long as you will finish”. Similar: “provided that”.
examples: You can borrow my car as long as you drive carefully.
As long as we leave by eight, we'll be fine.
I don't mind what we eat, as long as it's not too spicy.
As long as you're happy, that's all that matters.

meaning: Means “only if” and introduces a condition.
usage: Formal to neutral. Common in contracts and rules. Variants: “providing that”, “provided”.
examples: You can take the exam again provided that you pay the fee.
Provided that the weather is good, the event will be held outdoors.
Staff may work from home provided that their manager agrees.
I'll lend you the money provided that you pay me back next month.

meaning: Introduces a possible situation that you are preparing for.
usage: Followed by a present tense for future meaning. It does not mean “if”: “Take an umbrella in case it rains” means take one now as a precaution.
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
I'll write down my number in case you need it.
We booked an extra room in case more people come.
Save your work regularly in case the computer crashes.

meaning: Introduces what will happen if something is not done, or means “apart from that”.
usage: Very common in warnings and advice: “Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late.”
examples: We need to leave now. Otherwise, we'll miss the train.
Write it down; otherwise, you'll forget.
The ending was disappointing. Otherwise, it was a great book.
Book early, otherwise the tickets will sell out.

meaning: Introduces the first in a series of points or actions.
usage: Common in speech and presentations. Often followed by “secondly” or “then”. In writing, “firstly” or “first” is shorter.
examples: First of all, I'd like to thank everyone for coming.
First of all, check that the machine is switched off.
There are two problems. First of all, it's too expensive.
First of all, let me explain why we're here.

meaning: Describes what finally happened after a long process or many changes.
usage: Do not confuse with “at the end” (of a period or place): “at the end of the film”.
examples: We looked at ten flats, and in the end we chose the first one.
In the end, the match was cancelled because of the rain.
She hesitated for weeks, but in the end she accepted the offer.
In the end, it didn't matter who was right.

chunk: At the end of the day, …
meaning: Introduces what you consider the most important fact after everything has been considered.
usage: Informal and spoken. Very common, but avoid it in formal writing, where it sounds like a cliché.
examples: At the end of the day, it's your decision.
At the end of the day, what matters is that everyone is safe.
We can discuss it all week, but at the end of the day we need to choose.
At the end of the day, money isn't everything.

meaning: Adds a surprising or more detailed fact, often one that contradicts what someone expects.
usage: Neutral. Similar to “Actually” or “In fact”.
examples: “Have you been to Rome?” “As a matter of fact, I lived there for two years.”
As a matter of fact, I was just about to call you.
It isn't difficult at all. As a matter of fact, it's quite easy.
As a matter of fact, the meeting has been cancelled.

meaning: Introduces the particular subject you are talking about.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Often introduces a strength or weakness: “When it comes to cooking, he's hopeless.”
examples: When it comes to cooking, my brother is the expert.
When it comes to saving money, I'm not very good.
She's very confident when it comes to public speaking.
When it comes to choosing a university, location matters.

meaning: Introduces a new subject that is connected to what was said before.
usage: Often used to move from one person or item in a list to another. Can sound dismissive: “As for him, I don't care what he thinks.”
examples: The food was great. As for the service, it was a bit slow.
I'm staying here. As for Tom, he's going home.
As for the budget, we'll discuss it next week.
Most students passed. As for the rest, they can retake the exam.

meaning: Means “without being affected by” something.
usage: Followed by a noun or a question word clause: “regardless of what people say”. Do not use the non-standard “irregardless”.
examples: Everyone is welcome, regardless of age.
Regardless of the weather, the race will go ahead.
She always says what she thinks, regardless of what people say.
The law applies to everyone, regardless of their position.

meaning: Introduces a clearer explanation of something you have just said.
usage: Very common in speech, especially when you think you have been misunderstood.
examples: I'm not saying it's bad. What I mean is that it could be better.
What I mean is, we need more time, not more money.
Sorry, that came out wrong. What I mean is I'm worried about you.
What I mean is that the problem isn't new.

meaning: Introduces a simpler or more direct way of saying the same thing.
usage: Neutral and common in speech and writing. Often used to state the real implication of something.
examples: The company is restructuring. In other words, people will lose their jobs.
He's “between jobs” — in other words, he's unemployed.
Demand exceeds supply. In other words, there isn't enough to go round.
She said she'd think about it. In other words, probably not.

chunk: What I'm trying to say is …
meaning: Introduces another attempt to express an idea clearly, often a sensitive one.
usage: Informal and spoken. Shows that you are struggling to express yourself or want to avoid offence.
examples: What I'm trying to say is that I need some space.
What I'm trying to say is, we can't keep doing things the old way.
Sorry, I'm not explaining this well. What I'm trying to say is that I'm grateful.
What I'm trying to say is that the data doesn't support his conclusion.

meaning: Introduces the point or suggestion that you have been leading up to.
usage: Informal. Related question: “What are you getting at?”, which asks what someone is hinting at.
examples: What I'm getting at is that we might need to cut costs.
What I'm getting at is, does anyone actually use this feature?
What I'm getting at is that the timing is wrong, not the idea.
I'll be honest; what I'm getting at is that we need a new supplier.

chunk: Let me put it another way
meaning: Signals that you are going to explain the same idea differently because the first attempt was unclear.
usage: Common in teaching and presentations. Variant: “To put it another way, …”.
examples: Let me put it another way: if we don't act now, we'll lose the client.
That's not very clear, is it? Let me put it another way.
Let me put it another way. Would you pay that much for it?
Let me put it another way: the more you practise, the easier it gets.

meaning: Introduces a simple version of a complicated explanation.
usage: Neutral. Common in teaching, presentations and popular science. Also: “Simply put, …”.
examples: To put it simply, the company is spending more than it earns.
To put it simply, a vaccine trains your immune system.
To put it simply, we can't afford it.
To put it simply, the brain needs sleep to store memories.

meaning: Introduces a more exact version of what you have just said.
usage: Neutral to formal. Common in academic and technical contexts. Variant: “More precisely, …”.
examples: The meeting is next week; to be more precise, on Tuesday afternoon.
Sales fell last year. To be more precise, they fell by twelve per cent.
He's from the north of England; to be more precise, from Leeds.
The problem is in the software or, to be more precise, in one small part of it.

meaning: Introduces an example that illustrates a general point.
usage: Often used at the start of a sentence after a general claim. Also: “Take … for instance.”
examples: Prices have risen sharply. Take housing, for example.
Some jobs are disappearing. Take bank clerks, for example.
Not all old buildings are protected. Take this one, for example.
Take my sister, for example: she changed careers at forty.

chunk: Let me give you an example
meaning: Introduces an example to make an explanation clearer.
usage: Common in presentations, teaching and interviews.
examples: Small changes can make a big difference. Let me give you an example.
Let me give you an example of what I mean.
That probably sounds abstract, so let me give you an example.
Let me give you an example from my last job.

meaning: Introduces the most important fact or argument, often after a digression.
usage: Informal to neutral. Often followed by a comma in speech: “The point is, …”. Can sound impatient.
examples: The point is, we don't have enough money.
I don't care who broke it. The point is that it needs fixing.
The point is that nobody asked the students what they wanted.
The point is, you should have told me earlier.

meaning: Introduces a statement that removes any possible misunderstanding.
usage: Neutral. Common in meetings and emails. Can sound firm when used to set limits.
examples: Just to be clear, the deadline is Friday, not Monday.
Just to be clear, I'm not blaming anyone.
Just to be clear, this offer is only for new customers.
Just to be clear, are we meeting at the office or online?

meaning: Introduces a question or statement that checks or explains a detail.
usage: Neutral and polite. Often used to check your understanding without sounding critical.
examples: Just to clarify, do you want the report in English or French?
Just to clarify, the price includes tax.
Just to clarify, we're talking about next year's budget, right?
Just to clarify, I didn't say the plan was wrong.

chunk: Do you see what I mean?
meaning: Checks whether the listener has understood your point.
usage: Informal. Often shortened to “See what I mean?”, which can also mean “I told you so.”
examples: It's not the price; it's the quality. Do you see what I mean?
If we change one part, everything else changes too. Do you see what I mean?
He's polite, but he never really listens. Do you see what I mean?
Do you see what I mean? The colours don't match.

meaning: Checks whether your explanation was clear.
usage: Very common in teaching, meetings and instructions. It sounds friendlier than “Do you understand?”.
examples: You fill in this form first, then send it to HR. Does that make sense?
Does that make sense, or shall I explain it again?
So the price depends on the season. Does that make sense?
I know it's complicated. Does that make sense so far?

meaning: Checks that the listener is following your explanation.
usage: Informal. Common in teaching. Also used to ask whether someone supports you: “Are you with me on this?”
examples: First we add the numbers, then we divide by three. Are you with me?
Are you with me so far?
This part is a bit tricky. Are you with me?
I'll go through it slowly. Are you with me?

meaning: Checks whether you have understood someone's meaning, often with surprise or disagreement.
usage: Can sound challenging, depending on intonation. Softer: “Do you mean that …?”.
examples: Are you saying that we have to start again?
Are you saying that I'm wrong?
Are you saying that the shop won't give me a refund?
Sorry, are you saying that the meeting is cancelled?

meaning: Summarizes someone's point to check that you have understood it.
usage: Common in meetings and negotiations. It can sound sarcastic if the summary is deliberately extreme.
examples: So what you're saying is that we need another week.
So what you're saying is, the price will go up next year?
So what you're saying is that the problem is the design, not the material.
So what you're saying is we should hire more staff?

meaning: Introduces your understanding of what someone has said, so that they can confirm or correct it.
usage: Polite and fairly formal. Common in meetings and interviews.
examples: If I understand you correctly, you'd like to change the contract.
If I understand you correctly, the delivery will arrive tomorrow.
If I understand you correctly, you're not happy with the service.
So, if I understand you correctly, the main issue is staffing?

chunk: What exactly do you mean by …?
meaning: Asks someone to explain a word or idea they have used.
usage: Can be neutral or challenging, depending on tone. Common in academic discussions.
examples: What exactly do you mean by “flexible hours”?
What exactly do you mean by that?
What exactly do you mean by success?
Sorry, what exactly do you mean by a “small change”?

meaning: Politely says that you did not hear or understand what someone said.
usage: Common on the phone and in noisy places. Often followed by a request: “Could you repeat it?”
examples: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again?
Sorry, I didn't catch that; the line's very bad.
Sorry, I didn't catch that last part.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. What was your name again?

meaning: Asks someone to repeat what they have just said.
usage: Polite and neutral. More polite: “Would you mind repeating that?”
examples: Sorry, could you say that again?
Could you say that again, a bit more slowly?
Could you say that again? I want to write it down.
I missed the number. Could you say that again?

chunk: Could you be a bit more specific?
meaning: Asks someone to give more details or a clearer example.
usage: Polite. Common in meetings, interviews and customer service.
examples: You said there were problems. Could you be a bit more specific?
Could you be a bit more specific about the dates?
I'd like to help. Could you be a bit more specific?
Could you be a bit more specific about what went wrong?

meaning: Politely says that you do not understand an explanation.
usage: Polite and indirect. Also: “I don't quite follow.” “Follow” here means “understand”.
examples: Sorry, I'm not sure I follow. Why do we need a second meeting?
I'm not sure I follow. Could you explain that again?
I'm not sure I follow your argument.
I'm not sure I follow; what does this have to do with the budget?

meaning: Introduces a summary of a situation to check that you understand it, often because it seems surprising or unfair.
usage: Informal. Often signals disbelief or annoyance.
examples: Let me get this straight: you want me to work on Sunday for free?
Let me get this straight. You lost the keys and the spare set?
So, let me get this straight: the meeting is cancelled, but we still have to come in?
Let me get this straight; who's paying for all this?

meaning: Says that you no longer understand what someone is explaining.
usage: Informal and polite. Shows that the explanation, not you, became hard to follow.
examples: Sorry, I'm a bit lost. Which form do I fill in first?
Sorry, I'm a bit lost. Who's Mark again?
Sorry, I'm a bit lost; can we go back to the second slide?
Sorry, I'm a bit lost. How did you get that number?

chunk: Could you run that by me again?
meaning: Asks someone to explain or repeat something.
usage: Informal. “Run something by someone” also means to tell them about it to get their opinion.
examples: Sorry, could you run that by me again?
Could you run that by me again? I missed the bit about the dates.
That's a lot of information. Could you run that by me again?
Could you run that by me again, slowly this time?

meaning: Asks someone to explain what they mean.
usage: Informal and mainly British. Sounds curious rather than critical. Similar: “What do you mean?”
examples: “The trip was interesting.” “How do you mean?”
How do you mean, it's not finished?
“He's changed a lot.” “How do you mean?”
“It's a strange place.” “How do you mean? Strange in what way?”

meaning: Introduces a very short summary of something.
usage: Informal. Also: “to put it in a nutshell”.
examples: In a nutshell, the project was a success.
In a nutshell, we need more staff and more time.
That's the plan in a nutshell.
In a nutshell, she's leaving because she's not happy.

meaning: Adds an explanation or correction, or gives you time to think.
usage: Very common in informal speech. Also corrects a slip of the tongue: “It's on Tuesday, I mean Wednesday.”
examples: It's a nice flat. I mean, it's small, but it's in a great area.
I mean, what's the point of arguing?
Let's meet at six. I mean, half past six.
I mean, I like him, but I wouldn't want to work with him.

meaning: Signals that you are going to say something again in a clearer or more tactful way.
usage: Common when a first attempt sounded rude or unclear.
examples: That came out wrong. Let me rephrase that.
Let me rephrase that: I think there might be a better option.
Sorry, let me rephrase that question.
Let me rephrase that. How satisfied are you with the service?

meaning: Makes a polite request.
usage: Followed by an -ing form: “Would you mind closing the door?” To agree, say “No, not at all” or “Of course not”, because the literal question is whether you object.
examples: Would you mind closing the window?
Would you mind waiting a few minutes?
Would you mind not smoking here, please?
Would you mind sending me the file again?

meaning: Asks for permission politely.
usage: Followed by a present tense. “Would you mind if I …?” takes a past tense and is more polite. Answer “No, go ahead” to give permission.
examples: Do you mind if I open the window?
Do you mind if I sit here?
Do you mind if I ask you a personal question?
Do you mind if I leave a bit early today?

chunk: I was wondering if you could …
meaning: Makes a very polite, indirect request.
usage: The past continuous makes the request softer. Common when asking for a favour from someone you don't know well, or in emails.
examples: I was wondering if you could help me with my CV.
I was wondering if you could give me a lift to the station.
I was wondering if you could send me the slides from today's lecture.
I was wondering if you could cover my shift on Saturday.

meaning: Makes a polite request, often for something inconvenient.
usage: “Possibly” makes the request softer and acknowledges that it may be difficult.
examples: Could you possibly lend me some money until Friday?
Could you possibly turn the music down a little?
Could you possibly finish the report by tomorrow?
Could you possibly move your car? It's blocking the gate.

meaning: Makes a formal, impersonal request.
usage: Common in emails, at hotels and in customer service. Avoids directly asking a person to do something.
examples: Would it be possible to change my booking?
Would it be possible to have the room with a view?
Would it be possible to extend the deadline by a week?
Would it be possible to speak to the manager?

chunk: Is there any chance you could …?
meaning: Makes a polite request when you are not sure the person will be able to help.
usage: Informal to neutral. Suggests that you know the request is a lot to ask.
examples: Is there any chance you could pick me up from the airport?
Is there any chance you could look at my essay before Monday?
Is there any chance you could swap shifts with me?
Is there any chance you could send it today?

meaning: Makes a polite request by asking whether something is possible for the other person.
usage: Common in workplace emails and phone calls. Less direct than “Can you …?”
examples: Would you be able to join the call at three?
Would you be able to check these figures for me?
Would you be able to deliver on Saturday?
Would you be able to give me some feedback on my presentation?

chunk: Could you do me a favour?
meaning: Prepares the listener for a request for help.
usage: Informal. Usually followed by the actual request. British spelling: favour; American: favor.
examples: Could you do me a favour and feed my cat this weekend?
Could you do me a favour? I need someone to check my email before I send it.
Could you do me a favour and keep this a secret?
Could you do me a favour? Can you pick up some milk on your way home?

meaning: Asks for information politely, without assuming the person knows.
usage: Followed by an indirect question with normal word order: “Do you happen to know where the station is?” not “where is the station”.
examples: Do you happen to know where the nearest pharmacy is?
Do you happen to know what time the shop closes?
Do you happen to know if this bus goes to the airport?
Do you happen to know her phone number?

meaning: Asks for permission informally.
usage: Informal and very common. Followed by a present tense. Also: “Is it all right if I …?”
examples: Is it OK if I bring a friend?
Is it OK if I use your phone charger?
Is it OK if I hand the essay in on Monday?
Is it OK if I take a photo?

meaning: Offers to do something for someone politely.
usage: Polite and common in work and service situations. Less formal: “Do you want me to …?”
examples: Would you like me to carry that for you?
Would you like me to call you a taxi?
Would you like me to send you a copy of the contract?
Would you like me to explain it again?

meaning: Offers to do something or asks for advice about what to do.
usage: Mainly British. Followed by a bare infinitive. Also used for suggestions: “Shall we go?”
examples: Shall I open the window?
Shall I call you back later?
It's getting late. Shall I book a taxi?
Shall I bring anything to the party?

meaning: Offers to do something in an informal way.
usage: Informal. In fast speech it often sounds like “D'you want me to …?”.
examples: Do you want me to help you with the dishes?
Do you want me to drive?
Do you want me to talk to him for you?
Do you want me to come with you to the doctor's?

meaning: Asks someone to tell you something, often whether they need help.
usage: Very common at the end of emails and conversations. Also: “Let me know when …”, “Let me know what you think.”
examples: Let me know if you need any help.
Let me know if you can't make it.
Let me know if anything changes.
Let me know if you have any questions about the report.

meaning: Gives someone permission or encouragement to do something.
usage: Friendly and common in emails and hosting. Followed by a bare infinitive.
examples: Feel free to call me if you have any questions.
Feel free to help yourself to coffee.
Feel free to interrupt if something isn't clear.
Feel free to bring a friend.

meaning: Makes a suggestion about something to do together.
usage: Informal. It is not a real question about reasons. Followed by a bare infinitive.
examples: Why don't we get a takeaway tonight?
Why don't we ask Anna? She knows about computers.
Why don't we take a short break?
Why don't we meet halfway, in Leeds?

meaning: Makes a suggestion.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form: “How about going to the cinema?” Similar: “What about …?”
examples: How about going for a walk?
How about Friday instead?
How about asking your teacher for help?
How about a coffee before we start?

meaning: Makes a tentative, polite suggestion.
usage: Softer than “Let's …”. Common in meetings and when you are not sure others will agree.
examples: Maybe we could meet next week instead.
Maybe we could ask the client what they prefer.
Maybe we could split the cost.
Maybe we could try a different approach.

meaning: Makes a suggestion or gives advice indirectly.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Also: “Have you considered …?” (more formal).
examples: Have you thought about studying abroad?
Have you thought about asking for a pay rise?
Have you thought about the cost of moving?
Have you thought about taking a few days off?

chunk: It might be a good idea to …
meaning: Gives advice or a suggestion in a gentle, indirect way.
usage: Polite and tactful. Useful when advising someone senior or a stranger.
examples: It might be a good idea to book in advance.
It might be a good idea to check with your manager first.
It might be a good idea to back up your files.
It might be a good idea to take a jacket; it gets cold at night.

meaning: Gives advice by imagining yourself in the other person's situation.
usage: Uses the second conditional. “If I was you” is common in speech but less correct.
examples: If I were you, I'd take the job.
If I were you, I'd talk to her before making a decision.
If I were you, I'd get a second opinion.
If I were you, I'd leave early to avoid the traffic.

meaning: Gives advice or a warning politely and indirectly.
usage: Common in professional contexts. Despite its gentle form, it can be a firm suggestion.
examples: You might want to check the spelling before you send it.
You might want to bring an umbrella.
You might want to sit down for this news.
You might want to call ahead; they sometimes close early.

meaning: Gives strong advice or a warning, implying that something bad will happen otherwise.
usage: “'d better” is short for “had better”, but it refers to the present or future. Followed by a bare infinitive. Negative: “You'd better not …”.
examples: You'd better hurry or you'll miss the bus.
You'd better tell her the truth.
You'd better not be late again.
You'd better take your passport, just in case.

meaning: Asks whether someone would like to do something; makes an invitation.
usage: Informal and British. Followed by a noun or -ing form: “Do you fancy going out?”
examples: Do you fancy going to the cinema tonight?
Do you fancy a cup of tea?
Do you fancy coming with us to the beach?
Do you fancy getting something to eat after work?

meaning: Asks whether someone is willing or keen to do something.
usage: Informal. Followed by a noun or -ing form. Also used alone: “Are you up for it?”
examples: Are you up for a game of tennis this weekend?
Are you up for going out tonight?
We're going hiking on Saturday. Are you up for it?
Are you up for a challenge?

meaning: Asks whether a suggestion or plan is acceptable to someone.
usage: Informal to neutral. Common when proposing times or plans. Reply: “Sounds good.”
examples: How does Thursday at ten sound?
How does pizza sound?
We could leave at six. How does that sound?
How does a weekend in Paris sound?

meaning: Politely declines an invitation while showing that you would like to accept.
usage: Usually followed by a reason. A friendly way to say no.
examples: I'd love to, but I've got to work late.
“Are you coming to the party?” “I'd love to, but I'm away that weekend.”
I'd love to, but I can't afford it this month.
I'd love to, but I've already made plans.

meaning: Politely refuses a request or says that something is not possible.
usage: “I'm afraid” softens bad news and does not mean fear here.
examples: I'm afraid I can't come to the meeting tomorrow.
I'm afraid I can't give you a refund.
I'm afraid I can't help you with that.
I'm afraid I can't make it on Friday.

meaning: Politely refuses an offer of help or a gift.
usage: Usually followed by a short reason: “… but I'm fine”, “… but I can manage”.
examples: Thanks for the offer, but I can manage.
Thanks for the offer, but I've already booked a taxi.
Thanks for the offer, but I'd rather do it myself.
Thanks for the offer, but we've decided to go with another company.

chunk: I'd appreciate it if you could …
meaning: Makes a polite but firm request.
usage: Common in emails and formal speech. Depending on tone, it can sound like a complaint: “I'd appreciate it if you could knock first.”
examples: I'd appreciate it if you could reply by Friday.
I'd appreciate it if you could keep this between us.
I'd appreciate it if you could knock before coming in.
I'd appreciate it if you could send the invoice again.

meaning: An informal greeting that asks how someone is.
usage: Informal. A short answer is expected: “Not bad, thanks. You?” Can also ask about a specific activity: “How's the new job going?”
examples: Hi, Tom! How's it going?
“How's it going?” “Not bad, thanks. Busy as usual.”
How's it going with the new flat?
Hey, how's it going? I haven't seen you all week.

meaning: Says that you have not seen someone or done something for a long time.
usage: Informal. Often followed by “since”: “It's been ages since we last met.”
examples: Sarah! It's been ages! How are you?
It's been ages since I've been to the cinema.
It's been ages since we had a proper conversation.
Wow, it's been ages. You look great.

meaning: A friendly greeting for someone you have not seen for a long time.
usage: Informal and humorous. Grammatically unusual, but it is a fixed expression.
examples: Hey, Mark! Long time no see!
Long time no see! What have you been doing?
“Long time no see!” “I know, it must be two years.”
Well, long time no see. Are you still living in Manchester?

chunk: What have you been up to?
meaning: Asks someone what they have been doing recently.
usage: Informal. Common when meeting a friend after some time. Reply: “Not much” or details of your recent life.
examples: It's great to see you! What have you been up to?
So, what have you been up to since we last met?
“What have you been up to?” “Oh, just working, mostly.”
What have you been up to lately? You look really well.

chunk: I've heard a lot about you
meaning: A friendly thing to say when you meet someone for the first time whom others have talked about.
usage: Polite. Often followed by “all good, I promise” as a joke. Common when meeting a partner's family or friends.
examples: Nice to meet you at last. I've heard a lot about you.
I've heard a lot about you from Emma.
“This is my boss, Anna.” “Hello! I've heard a lot about you.”
I've heard a lot about you, all good things, of course.

meaning: Thanks a host for inviting you to their home, event or programme.
usage: Said when leaving someone's home or at the start or end of an interview or podcast. Reply: “Thanks for coming.”
examples: Thanks for having me. I had a lovely evening.
Thanks for having me on the show.
Thanks for having me for the weekend; it was great.
“Thanks for having me.” “Any time. Come again soon.”

meaning: Expresses sincere thanks for someone's help or kindness.
usage: Slightly warmer than “Thank you”. Often follows “Thanks”: “Thanks, I really appreciate it.”
examples: Thanks for helping me move. I really appreciate it.
I know you're busy, so I really appreciate it.
Thanks for listening. I really appreciate it.
You didn't have to do that, but I really appreciate it.

meaning: Thanks someone for a favour and promises to help them in return.
usage: Informal. Also: “I owe you a drink”, “I owe you big time” (very informal).
examples: Thanks for covering for me. I owe you one.
You saved my life with that lift. I owe you one.
I owe you one for helping me with the move.
“I fixed your bike.” “Thanks! I owe you one.”

meaning: Thanks someone warmly for a gift or kind act that you did not expect.
usage: Polite and affectionate. It does not mean the person did something wrong. Usually followed by “Thank you!” or “It's lovely.”
examples: Flowers! Oh, you shouldn't have!
You shouldn't have, but thank you so much.
“I got you a little present.” “You shouldn't have!”
You shouldn't have gone to so much trouble.

meaning: A polite reply to thanks, meaning that it was no trouble.
usage: Slightly old-fashioned but still common. Alternatives: “You're welcome”, “No problem”, “Any time”.
examples: “Thanks for your help.” “Don't mention it.”
Don't mention it; I was happy to help.
“Thanks for the lift.” “Oh, don't mention it.”
Don't mention it. You'd do the same for me.

meaning: An informal reply to thanks or an apology, meaning that everything is fine.
usage: Informal and very common in British and Australian English. Avoid it in formal emails.
examples: “Sorry I'm late.” “No worries.”
“Thanks for the help.” “No worries!”
No worries, we can reschedule for next week.
“I forgot to bring your book.” “No worries, there's no rush.”

meaning: Says that something you are doing for someone is not inconvenient.
usage: Polite reply to thanks or an apology. Shorter: “No trouble.”
examples: “Are you sure you can drive me?” “It's no trouble at all.”
It's no trouble at all; I'm going that way anyway.
“Sorry to bother you.” “It's no trouble at all.”
Stay for dinner. It's no trouble at all.

meaning: Expresses sympathy when someone tells you bad news.
usage: Polite and neutral. “Sorry” here expresses sympathy, not an apology.
examples: “My grandfather is in hospital.” “I'm sorry to hear that.”
I'm sorry to hear that you didn't get the job.
“We split up last month.” “Oh, I'm sorry to hear that.”
I'm sorry to hear that you've been ill.

meaning: Shows empathy by recognizing that someone is in a difficult situation.
usage: Supportive and informal. Other adjectives are possible: “That must be really frustrating.”
examples: You're working and studying full-time? That must be really hard.
“My parents live on the other side of the world.” “That must be really hard.”
That must be really hard, especially with young children.
Moving to a new country alone? That must be really hard.

meaning: Shows sympathy by saying you have had a similar experience.
usage: Informal. Use with care: it can sound dismissive if you have not really had the same experience.
examples: “I'm so nervous about the interview.” “I know how you feel.”
I know how you feel; I failed my driving test twice.
I know how you feel. Mondays are the worst.
Believe me, I know how you feel.

meaning: Expresses disappointment or sympathy about something unfortunate.
usage: Here “shame” means “a pity”, not embarrassment. Also: “That's a shame.”
examples: “The concert's been cancelled.” “What a shame!”
What a shame you can't come to the party.
“It rained all weekend.” “Oh, what a shame!”
What a shame! I was really looking forward to it.

meaning: Expresses that you feel better because a worry has been removed.
usage: Informal. Stronger: “What a relief!”
examples: “The test results are fine.” “That's a relief.”
You found your passport? That's a relief!
“The flight's on time.” “Oh, that's a relief.”
That's a relief; I thought I'd lost all my work.

meaning: Praises someone for something they have done or decided.
usage: Informal and encouraging. With an ironic tone it can sound dismissive.
examples: “I've finally quit smoking.” “Good for you!”
You ran a marathon? Good for you!
“I told my boss I wanted a raise.” “Good for you!”
Good for you for standing up to him.

meaning: Expresses pleasure at someone's success or happy event.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Note the preposition: “on”, not “for”.
examples: Congratulations on your new job!
Congratulations on passing your exams!
Congratulations on the baby!
Congratulations on your engagement! When's the wedding?

meaning: Expresses hope that something will happen as you want.
usage: Informal. People sometimes cross their fingers as they say it. Also: “I'll keep my fingers crossed for you.”
examples: The results come out tomorrow. Fingers crossed!
Fingers crossed the weather stays dry for the wedding.
“Did you get the flat?” “Not yet. Fingers crossed.”
Fingers crossed it all goes well.

meaning: Wishes someone success with something they are about to do.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing form. Also: “Good luck in your exam” and “Best of luck!”
examples: Good luck with your interview!
Good luck with the move!
Good luck with finding a new job.
Good luck with the exams next week!

meaning: Says that you will pay for something, usually food or drinks.
usage: Informal. Also: “This one's on me”, “Lunch is on me.”
examples: Put your wallet away; it's on me.
Order whatever you like. It's on me tonight.
“How much do I owe you?” “Nothing, it's on me.”
